procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 22nd November, 1976 of the Punjab & Haryana High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 501 of 1973.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Trial Court acquitted the accused (appellants) of all charges. The State of Haryana appealed this acquittal to the Punjab & Haryana High Court (Criminal Appeal No. 501 of 1973). The High Court allowed the State's appeal, reversing the acquittal with respect to the appellants.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed the High Court's decision to the Supreme Court (Criminal Appeal No. 584 of 1976). The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction recorded by the High Court, and restored the appellants' acquittal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court, while reversing an acquittal, is required to deal with each of the reasons that prompted the trial court to record the acquittal and demonstrate how those reasons are incorrect.

facts: The trial court (Sessions Judge) acquitted the appellants, providing elaborate and substantial reasons for its decision after analyzing the prosecution's evidence.
The State appealed this acquittal to the High Court.
The High Court reversed the acquittal and convicted the appellants.

In its decision, the High Court did not deal with or discuss the specific reasons the trial court gave for the acquittal. Instead, it was primarily influenced by the nature of the injuries on the deceased's body.
law: The Supreme Court established a clear duty for a High Court when it is considering an appeal against an acquittal.
The High Court is required to deal with each of the reasons that prompted the trial court to acquit the accused.
Furthermore, the High Court must demonstrate how, if at all, the trial court's reasons were wrong or incorrect.
A High Court cannot reverse an acquittal without undertaking this specific exercise.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court in this case failed to perform its required duty.
The High Court was found to be "clearly in error" because it reversed the acquittal without discussing or refuting any of the substantial reasons provided by the Sessions Judge.
Instead of engaging with the trial court's detailed reasoning, the High Court based its decision to convict almost solely on its own interpretation of the injuries found on the deceased.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that because the High Court did not deal with the trial court's reasons for acquittal and demonstrate how they were incorrect, it could not legally reverse the acquittal. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's conviction and restored the trial court's acquittal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court, while reversing an acquittal, is required to deal with each of the reasons that prompted the trial court to record the acquittal and demonstrate how those reasons are incorrect.
appellant_arguments: The High Court reversed the acquittal without dealing with or discussing the substantial reasons given by the Sessions Judge for acquitting the accused.
The High Court's duty was to deal with each reason that led to the acquittal and point out how those reasons were wrong or incorrect.
The High Court failed to undertake this necessary exercise and instead improperly relied on its own conjectures and surmises, particularly regarding the injuries on the deceased.
respondent_arguments: The High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal because the nature of the injuries on the deceased, particularly on the soles and buttocks, clearly indicated he had been beaten while in police custody.
The conclusion that the deceased was tortured was strengthened by the fact that one of the appellants deliberately tried to minimize the number of injuries in the inquest report.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When dealing with an appeal against an acquittal, the High Court must address each reason that prompted the trial court to record the acquittal and must demonstrate how those reasons were wrong or incorrect. The High Court cannot reverse an acquittal without undertaking this exercise.
obiter: The High Court was in error for relying solely on the nature of some injuries to conclude that the deceased must have been assaulted by the appellant in custody.
In doing so, the High Court indulged in conjectures and surmises.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The duty of the High Court while dealing with an appeal against acquittal is to deal with each one of the reasons which prompted the trial court to record the acquittal and to point out how, if at all, those reasons were wrong or incorrect. The High Court cannot reverse an acquittal without undertaking such an exercise.
legal_tests_applied: When reviewing an appeal against acquittal, the appellate court must deal with each reason that prompted the trial court to record the acquittal and demonstrate how those reasons are wrong or incorrect.
